html:
The Ye'kwana, who call themselves So'to, are a Carib-speaking Indigenous people of the upper Orinoco, Ventuari and Caura rivers in southern Venezuela, with a few villages in Brazil.

They are famous canoe builders and travellers who traded widely along the rivers, carrying goods between the Orinoco and the Amazon basin. Their villages centre on a large round house whose roof is built as a model of the sky. Their sacred stories, gathered in the book Watunna, tell how the world was made and how the first trickster brought the Ye'kwana their crops.

Their neighbours are the Sanema, a branch of the Yanomami. In the 1700s they fought off Spanish attempts to build forts and missions on their rivers, and they kept their lands into modern times, though gold miners now press into them. The Warao of the delta and the Pemon of the Gran Sabana are other peoples of the region.
sum: The Ye'kwana, who call themselves So'to, are a Carib-speaking Indigenous people of the upper Orinoco, Ventuari and Caura rivers in southern Venezuela, with a few villages in Brazil.
